html:
The Selk'nam, also called the Ona, were the people of the main island of Tierra del Fuego, at the southern tip of South America, now split between Argentina and Chile. They hunted guanaco on foot with bows and arrows, wore guanaco skins and lived in small family bands. Their great ceremony, the Hain, initiated young men and was famous for its painted masked figures.

The island got its name when Magellan's crew saw their fires from the strait in 1520. Their neighbours were the Tehuelche to the north and canoe peoples of the channels such as the Yaghan, part of the shellfish and marine mammal hunters of the far south.

They kept their independence until the 1880s. Then gold seekers and sheep ranchers took the island, and hired men hunted the Selk'nam down, a killing now called the Selk'nam genocide. Survivors were sent to missions, where disease killed most of them. Their descendants today work to revive the culture.
